cues.text: Chapter five: metrics and tools.
Let us begin with the numbers a team uses to see how its work is flowing.
The first is velocity.
Velocity is the number of completed story points per sprint for one team, and it uses that team's own estimation scale.
Take an example: a team completes 18, then 20, then 22 story points in three sprints.
The mean is 20.
Notice how carefully the source frames this.
That mean of 20 is not a promise of what the team will deliver next, and it is not a way to rank one team against another.
Two teams estimate in their own units, so their velocities simply cannot be compared.
Next, two charts that show progress.
A burndown chart plots remaining work.
A burnup chart plots completed work together with total scope.
Why does that matter?
Because the burnup chart is useful for distinguishing scope change.
If the total scope line rises, you can see that the work grew, rather than wrongly concluding the team slowed down.
Now we move to flow measures, and here the vocabulary needs care.
Throughput is the number of items completed per unit of time.
Lead time is often measured from request to delivery.
Cycle time runs from work start to finish, and the source stresses that you must define the boundary, meaning exactly where the clock starts and stops.
Then there is WIP, work in progress, which counts work that has been started but not yet finished.
These measures connect through Little's Law.
Under stable system assumptions, WIP equals throughput multiplied by average cycle time.
Here is the worked example.
If throughput is 4 items per day and average WIP is 12, then average cycle time is approximately 3 days, because 12 divided by 4 is 3.
The qualification is important: do not apply this to unstable flow without caution.
The law rests on the system being stable.
And speed is never the whole picture.
A team should also monitor blockers, defects, customer value and quality, as well as speed.
Now let us turn to tools and practices.
Jira and Trello style boards track the backlog and status of work, along with acceptance criteria, ownership and dependencies.
So a board is where a team sees what is waiting, what is underway, who owns it, what conditions define it as acceptable, and what it depends on.
Then there is the retrospective.
A retrospective asks four things: what worked, what did not work, what specific experiment will be tried and who owns it, and what the follow-up will be.
The experiment and the owner should be specific, so improvement does not stay a vague wish.
Finally, collaboration.
Pairing, review and cross-functional collaboration reduce handoff delay, because work waits less when fewer separate hands must pass it along.
And the closing principle ties everything together.
Agile metrics should improve systems, not punish individuals for story-point counts.
Measures exist to help the team see and fix how the work flows, never to blame the people doing it.
